extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and research-integrity professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Indicators, publisher responses, and suggested controls for identifying scholarly papers that may be unreliable (e.g., due to compromised peer review, paper mills, automated/machine-translated text, or citation manipulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromised peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review process has been manipulated or bypassed (e.g., fake reviews, reviewer identity problems, or otherwise corrupted review workflows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions were issued after the publisher identified compromised peer review; compromised review can be effected via fake reviewer identities or manipulated guest-edited issues. Look for signs such as unusually rapid acceptance, improbable reviewer reports, or evidence of fake reviewer accounts. The article notes publishers investigate using intelligence and whistleblower information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake peer reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit occurrence of fabricated reviewer reports or fraudulent reviewer identities used to rubber-stamp papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publisher described use of 'fake peer reviews' as a mechanism paper mills used to evade quality control. Detection strategies include checking reviewer emails/affiliations, cross-checking reviewer identities, and using editorial oversight for guest issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate or irrelevant references
rubrics_metrics.description: References that are irrelevant, incorrectly placed, or otherwise inappropriate for the claims made in the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noted as a reason for retraction; authors may allege technical reference-management errors, but inappropriate placement or irrelevant citations are red flags for unreliable scholarship. Check that citations actually support the cited claims and that reference placement is coherent with the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsensical phrases / 'tortured phrases' indicating blind use of AI or machine translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Odd, unnatural, or 'tortured' wording that suggests text was produced or heavily altered by AI or poor machine translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guillaume Cabanac's 'tortured phrases' detector flagged many articles for odd language; such phrases (nonsensical or oddly substituted terminology) can indicate papermill or automated text-generation. Use language-anomaly screening tools and manual inspection for recurring strange phrase patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undeclared use of AI in the publication process
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors or submissions use AI tools (for writing, translation, or editing) without disclosure, leading to questionable text quality or integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Springer Nature flagged 'increase in undeclared use of AI' as a significant threat. Undeclared AI use may produce hallucinations, incoherent phrasing, or mismatched citations; require disclosure and screen for AI-generated patterns where policy mandates transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper mill origin / papermill submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles originated from commercial paper mills that sell authorship slots, write papers, or manufacture citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper mills often produce batches of similar/low-quality manuscripts, sometimes exploiting guest-edited collections and compromised peer review. Indicators include repeated odd phrasing across papers, similar reference patterns, and coordinated authorship/citation patterns. Investigations may rely on whistleblowers and automated detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest-edited collections vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Guest-edited special issues or collections that allow lower editorial oversight and can be exploited to publish low-quality or fraudulent papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher noted paper mills used guest-edited collections and fake peer reviews to evade quality control. As a mitigation, policies may forbid unsolicited guest proposals, require an editorial board member or Editor-in-Chief on guest editor teams, and strengthen front-end screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anomalous citation behavior (excessive self-citation and citation stacking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation patterns that deviate from norms, including disproportionate journal self-citation and citation exchanges between journals (citation stacking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarivate suppresses journals from Journal Citation Reports for 'anomalous citation behavior.' Monitor citation distributions for excessive self-citation rates, reciprocal citation clusters, or other network anomalies that may indicate manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate manipulation of citation counts or patterns to inflate metrics (e.g., excessive journal self-citation, citation stacking between journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can lead to loss of Journal Impact Factor and be a reason for scrutiny or corrective action. Use bibliometric analysis and editorial checks to detect suspicious citation rings or unusual citation spikes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicious or non-institutional author/reviewer contact details
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of non-institutional email addresses (e.g., Gmail, Yahoo) for authors or reviewers that may indicate lower traceability or fabricated identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters noted anomaly detection could flag non-institutional addresses as a basic screening step. While not definitive alone, multiple non-institutional contacts across a collection is a red flag to investigate further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language quality alone is not definitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-native-English authors or use of editing tools can produce imperfect English, but poor language alone does not prove misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argued that use of Grammarly or paid language-editing services can explain some phrasing issues; assess substantive coherence, citation validity, and review traces in addition to language quality before concluding misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of suspicious citation/reference patterns across many papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring problematic citations, misplaced references, or consistent bibliographic anomalies across multiple papers in a journal or collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large numbers of similar reference issues across a journal (as flagged on PubPeer) suggest systemic problems such as papermills or editorial failure. Conduct cross-paper bibliographic analysis to identify patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight and turnover as risk factors
rubrics_metrics.description: High editor turnover, absent or weak editorial board oversight, or failure to respond to complaints can coincide with increased publication of problematic papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents recent editor turnover at several journals where mass retractions occurred. Strengthening editorial governance and clear responsibility for guest issues can reduce risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-end research-integrity screening tools at submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of automated and manual integrity tools during submission (plagiarism checks, language/anomaly detectors, citation analysis) to detect problematic papers early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Springer Nature reported adding new tools to the submission front end. Recommended practice: implement multi-modal screening (text anomalies, authorship checks, citation/network analysis) prior to peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy controls for guest-edited issues (no unsolicited proposals; editorial board involvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational policies to prevent exploitation of guest-edited issues: forbidding unsolicited guest proposals and requiring an editorial board member or Editor-in-Chief as part of the guest-editor team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher instituted these rules as part of strengthened processes for guest-edited issues. Such policies increase accountability and reduce the ability of paper mills to place content via special issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research-integrity training for editorial board members
rubrics_metrics.description: Mandatory training for editorial board members in research integrity practices and detection of problematic submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher reported extensive research integrity training for board members; training should cover spotting fake reviews, papermill signs, citation anomalies, and appropriate escalation procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of whistleblower intelligence and confidential investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on third-party tips and confidential inquiries when investigating suspected misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher cited whistleblower information and past work intelligence as sources; confidentiality is maintained during investigations to avoid alerting bad actors. Encourage channels for secure reporting and triage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of reviewer comments is not a sole proof of review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of many reviewer comments (e.g., 'Reviewers made a total of 23 comments') does not alone prove peer-review integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors cited numerous reviewer comments to defend review legitimacy, but publishers and investigators should assess the substance, identity, and independence of reviewers rather than counting comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceable researcher/reviewer identifiers (e.g., ORCiD) to improve accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of persistent, verifiable identifiers for authors and reviewers to increase traceability and reduce anonymity-based fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters advocated ORCiD and even traceable ledgers/blockchains as means to maintain integrity. Implementing verified identifiers helps detect fabricated identities and improves transparency in editorial workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication anomaly detection (basic checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple automated checks such as email-domain screening, language-anomaly detection, and bibliographic sanity checks as first-line defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters recommended basic anomaly detection (e.g., flagging Gmail/Yahoo addresses) as inexpensive measures that would likely have caught many problems before publication. Combine with deeper checks for higher-risk submissions.
